title: Add Megawatt-Hours to Already-Interconnected Batteries
one_liner: The queue limits megawatts, not megawatt-hours, so sell cheap add-on energy blocks to existing 2-hour battery and solar sites that already own the grid connection.
customer: Owners of 2019-2024 vintage 2-hour storage and solar sites (IPPs, infrastructure funds, utilities) in PJM, ERCOT and CAISO. Storage developers and data center developers who lack queue positions are the second buyer group.
problem: New MW wait years in interconnection queues. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh and new projects average 3.5 hours. Existing 2-hour fleets are under-accredited for capacity, and their owners are not thinking about bolt-on energy.
solution: Engineer and finance duration uplift by adding DC-coupled or AC-block MWh behind the existing inverters and point of interconnection. Provide standardized BMS integration and warranty tooling. Second product: use surplus interconnection headroom at solar and wind farms to add storage MW, with a revenue share to the site owner. The company screens sites from public data, packages them and sells them or builds them.
why_now: Cell prices collapsed. Capacity prices at the cap reward accredited duration. Regulators (surplus interconnection service, MISO ERAS, PJM RRI) are openly trying to reuse existing grid connections.
revenue_model: Engineering and development fee per kWh added, a share of incremental capacity revenue, or resale of ready-to-build projects.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the interconnection agreement, not the battery. Every existing 2-hour battery is a queue position with half its energy potential unused, and it is the one capacity addition that skips the queue.
first_30_days: List ~200 US storage projects at 2 hours or less from EIA-860 and ISO data. Model uplift economics for 10 of them under PJM and ERCOT rules. Send owners a one-page 'what two more hours earns you' analysis. Sign two or three paid feasibility studies. Line up a non-FEOC DC block supplier.

title: Battery Passport Onboarding for E-Bike and Storage Makers
one_liner: Done-for-you EU battery passport, QR labelling and supplier data collection for makers of e-bikes, scooters and industrial or stationary batteries facing the 18 Feb 2027 date.
customer: Mid-size e-bike, e-scooter and light-EV brands, industrial battery pack assemblers and BESS integrators selling in the EU (20-500 staff), plus importers who count as the manufacturer.
problem: The EU Battery Regulation requires from 18 Feb 2027 a QR code and electronic battery passport for EV, light-transport and industrial batteries above 2 kWh (background knowledge; verify current status and any slippage). The data spans composition, cell supplier, recycled content, carbon footprint and state of health, and it must be extracted from cell makers who resist sharing. Larger passport vendors serve automakers and big OEMs, so small assemblers fall through.
solution: A supplier data-collection portal with templates for cell makers, a passport record generator with public and restricted access tiers, QR label files, state-of-health data hooks, a compliance checklist and change updates, plus a service layer that chases suppliers until they answer.
why_now: About 20 weeks remain, delegated acts and standards are still in flux, and small makers cannot wait for perfect specs. Even if parts slip, buyers still need the underlying data.
revenue_model: EUR 8-30k onboarding plus EUR 3-10k/year platform per battery family, with supplier-chasing billed hourly.
non_obvious_insight: The passport is a supplier-data-chasing problem, not a blockchain problem. Small buyers can pool leverage as a buying club so a cell maker answers one questionnaire instead of fifty.
first_30_days: Compile 200 EU e-bike and light-EV brands via a trade body and email a 'passport readiness scorecard'. Sign five design partners at EUR 5k and negotiate a template data sheet with two cell makers.

title: Condo Vote Toolkit for Tourist-Flat Bans
one_liner: A compliant e-vote, notice and evidence kit that lets condo communities decide the fate of tourist flats building by building, sold to the property administrators who run those votes.
customer: Property administrators who manage 50-300 buildings each (administradores de fincas in Spain, condominium managers in Brazil) and other managers in cities with short-term-rental limits. Later, mid-term-let operators and hosts who need a 'yes' vote (a firewalled second product).
problem: Tourism regulation is moving from city hall to the building's owners' assembly. Brazil (May 2026) requires 2/3 condo-owner approval, Madrid bans listings without a private entrance, and Barcelona bans all short-term rentals from Nov 2028 (Palma already has a full ban). Spain's 2025 condo-law change also gave owner communities a say over tourist flats (from my knowledge, verify locally). Each vote needs proper notice, quorum, minutes and bylaw amendments. Administrators run this on paper and email, and challenged votes get annulled on procedure.
solution: A per-building workspace with a jurisdiction-specific notice-and-quorum engine, proof of delivery, proxy voting, minutes generation, and local-language bylaw templates approved by local counsel. It adds an incident log (noise, keys, trash) with timestamped evidence and standard letters, plus a 'what is still allowed' guide for converting to compliant mid-term leases.
why_now: Bans and consent rules landing in 2025-2026 force thousands of building-level decisions in the next 12-24 months. Spain's $75M fine on Airbnb (Dec 2025) shows enforcement is real. Stranded short-stay inventory means every owner must choose between a ban and conversion.
revenue_model: About EUR 149 per vote packet, or EUR 2 per unit per month for administrator firms. A separate host-side package (consent-campaign management) at about EUR 500 per approved building, kept firewalled from the neutral tool.
non_obvious_insight: The fight over overtourism has moved to the general assembly of a single building. The buyer who feels the pain is the administrator exposed when a vote is challenged, and no legal-tech vendor sells to these mostly paper-based professionals.
first_30_days: Start with Spain. Build the vote checklist, notice templates and minutes generator in spreadsheets and documents. Offer them to 10 administrators in Barcelona, Madrid and Valencia via the professional-college newsletter at EUR 149 per vote, and aim for 5 paid votes. Automate whichever step they complain about most.

title: Resin Swap Bureau for Shortage-Hit Molders
one_liner: Fast material-equivalency testing and paperwork for injection molders who must switch resin grades when supply breaks.
customer: Small and mid-size injection molders and extruders with 10-200 employees, and their OEM quality engineers (appliance, auto, medical, electrical).
problem: Hormuz transits run about 10 a day against a baseline of 88-130, and the Gulf is a large polymer and petrochemical exporter (my inference on resin exposure). ISM comments cite long lead times and price volatility. Molders forced to change resin need to requalify with UL recognition, food-contact letters, PPAP and customer sign-off, and testing labs take weeks.
solution: An equivalency database (datasheet parsing plus coupon results) and a fast-turn lab partner. For each part spec it ranks substitutes, runs a five-day test protocol (tensile, impact, heat deflection, melt flow, shrinkage, UL 94 screen, color), and produces the change package: process change notice, PPAP delta and customer approval draft. It tracks UL, FDA and REACH status.
why_now: The war shock and volatility force substitutions now, and lead times are stretching. Molders have no in-house materials engineers.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k per part-family qualification. About $6k a year for database and alerts. Margin on lab work.
non_obvious_insight: In a shortage, finding a substitute resin is easy because a distributor can suggest one. The bottleneck is proving to a customer's QA that the substitute is allowed. The valuable product is the paperwork.
first_30_days: Partner with a certified test lab. Sign five molders. Build the first 50 equivalency sets in one resin family (PP, ABS or PC) from public datasheets. Publish a free shortage swap guide to gather leads.

title: Yield Twins and Robotic Cells for Regional Beef Packers
one_liner: Start with 3D vision yield scoring on the fabrication line and grow into robotic trimming cells for independent packers.
customer: Independent regional beef packers processing under about 2,000 head a day.
problem: Record cattle prices and a 75-year-low herd squeeze packer margins, while skilled knife labor is scarce and immigration enforcement hits meatpacking labor hardest.
solution: A camera-based yield-and-trim-loss scoring system for cut optimization, then robotic primal trimming and portioning cells sold as a service.
why_now: Physical-AI and 3D-vision costs dropped in 2025-26, and thin packer margins make a 1% yield gain worth millions.
revenue_model: Software at $2-4k per month per line first, then per-head fees for robotic cells.
non_obvious_insight: With margins this thin, the software yield gain pays before any robot works, and the data it collects trains the robot.
first_30_days: Visit three independent packers, mount cameras on a fab line, and deliver a first weekly yield report as a paid pilot.

title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.

title: Disaster-Day Instant Cash Parametric Cover
one_liner: Pay a fixed sum to a household's phone within hours of an official evacuation order or multi-day power shutoff, funded by cheap capital that is hunting for granular parametric risk.
customer: Employers, HOAs, utilities, school districts and credit unions in wildfire, flood and hurricane zones that buy group cover for employees or members. Also mortgage servicers for at-risk borrowers.
problem: After an evacuation order, households spend hundreds of dollars a day on hotels, fuel, food and pet boarding before any additional-living-expense claim is paid. Renters and FAIR plan or nonrenewed homeowners often lack that cover entirely. Claims take weeks.
solution: A parametric micro-policy paying $500-$2,000 within hours when an official evacuation order, extended power shutoff, or verified flood depth covers the insured address. Triggers come from public alert feeds and utility notices, and payment goes to a debit card or wallet. An MGA fronts it with ILS-backed capacity.
why_now: Reinsurance is softening and cat bond capital is at a record ($65.6B outstanding), so granular parametric capacity is cheap. Instant rails are mature, and nonrenewals and FAIR plan reliance are growing.
revenue_model: $5-$15 per household per month, an MGA margin of 20-30%, and group distribution fees.
non_obvious_insight: Instant cash, not indemnity, is the product, and small payouts make basis risk tolerable. Institutions with a duty of care buy per head, so a single sale reaches hundreds of households.
first_30_days: Pilot with a rural credit union and one WUI-county employer or school district. Find a parametric MGA to front it, run a synthetic-trigger payout test, and sign a paid 90-day pilot.

title: Price-Raise Autopilot for One-Person Service Firms
one_liner: Find the underpriced clients in a solo operator's own invoice history and execute personalized price increases, paid as a share of the uplift.
customer: Nonemployer and 1-5 person service businesses with 50-800 repeat clients: groomers, cleaners, landscapers, bookkeepers, tutors, therapists, detailers.
problem: Rising costs are the top financial challenge, yet most solo operators have not repriced in years because they fear churn. The industry sells lead generation, not repricing, even though a modest increase on the bottom 40% of clients often beats a 20% lift in leads.
solution: Connect Stripe, Square, QuickBooks, Jobber or booking-software history. For each client, compute the effective hourly rate after drive time, materials and discounts, and rank clients as safe-to-raise or protect. Draft one-to-one messages in the owner's voice, send by text or email, track churn and replies, and roll back individual clients if needed. The dashboard shows before-and-after profit per hour.
why_now: The Fed's 2026 survey shows 76% of international sourcers already passed costs to customers, so consumers now accept increases. Payment and booking APIs give clean multi-year history, and LLMs write natural personal notes at zero marginal cost.
revenue_model: 15-20% of first-year incremental revenue captured (no uplift, no fee), or a $49/month plan for owners who prefer flat pricing.
non_obvious_insight: The industry assumes the number-one problem, getting customers, is the one to fix. For a business of one, the fastest path to profit is charging existing customers correctly, and owners are too close to their clients to do it themselves. Outcome pricing also works because the owner sees the money.
first_30_days: Run a concierge version for 20 groomers, cleaners and landscapers found in local Facebook groups, using exports and spreadsheets. Measure revenue lift and churn below 3%. Publish two before-and-after case studies and use them to price the software.

title: Alt-Data From AI-Training Gig Workers
one_liner: A worker-owned pay-transparency panel for expert data contractors. Its aggregated signals on which domains are hiring, what they pay and how many hours exist become a leading-indicator dataset for investors and rival platforms.
customer: Hedge funds, VCs and AI-lab competitive-intelligence teams pay $30-150k a year for the index. Workers get the basic tier free or for $9-15 a month.
problem: Mercor's reported gross run rate went from about $0.5B to $2B in nine months, and the category claims millions of contractors, yet nobody outside the labs can see which skills are in demand or when a domain saturates. Workers complain of falling pay and have no rate data, while investors price a $10-25B category on anecdotes.
solution: A browser extension plus web app where contractors log, or auto-capture from their own dashboards, pay rate, hours offered, rejections and coarse project category (never confidential content). There is a public 'Levels.fyi for AI gigs' leaderboard by platform and domain, and a paid weekly index of hours availability and pay by domain, with saturation early-warnings.
why_now: The human-data market went from niche to multi-billion in a year, contractors are publicly vocal (HN, Verge, Wired coverage) and investor appetite for AI-adjacent labor data is high. No panel exists.
revenue_model: Institutional data subscriptions ($50-150k a year), a premium worker tier ($9-15 a month) and possibly sponsored placements from challenger platforms recruiting supply.
non_obvious_insight: Gig workers are usually treated as supply, but here they are a sensor network that reads the frontier labs' priorities weeks before any press release. Workers will join because it helps them negotiate and avoid saturated domains. Platforms can't easily object to workers sharing their own pay data, provided the design avoids NDA-covered project details.
first_30_days: Seed 300 members from data-annotation subreddits and Discords with a pay-rate survey. Publish a 'State of expert AI gig pay' report. Pitch 10 funds and 3 VC platform teams a sample weekly index, and land one paid pilot.

title: GST Credit Recovery on UPI Fees
one_liner: Recover the 18% GST on new UPI MDR fees as input credit for retailers and distributors that will otherwise never claim it.
customer: GST-registered mobile, FMCG and pharma retailers and distributors in India, and their chartered accountants.
problem: From Oct 15 the 0.4% MDR carries 18% GST, and AICPDF estimates a Rs 7,000-9,000 Cr burden on distributors. Small businesses will not reconcile bulk PSP fee invoices to GSTR-2B, so credit is left unclaimed.
solution: Ingest PSP settlement reports, match fee invoices to GSTR-2B, flag missing credits and produce claim workpapers for CAs. Composition-scheme dealers are ineligible and must be screened out. The wedge is retailer associations already mobilising over the fee.
why_now: MDR starts Oct 15 and retailer bodies are organised around a 'No UPI Day' on Oct 2.
revenue_model: 10-15% of recovered credit, or Rs 499-1,999 per month per business.
non_obvious_insight: The protest is about the 0.4%. The GST layer is partly recoverable money nobody is discussing, and associations will trade it for a visible win for members.
first_30_days: Build reconciliation for PhonePe and Paytm settlement file formats and sign two retailer associations.

title: Legal Defense Plan for Human-in-the-Loop Workers
one_liner: A USCCA-style membership that protects the nurse, safety driver or loan officer who gets blamed when AI recommends and a human signs, plus an 'override receipt' log the member personally owns.
customer: Unions, state nurses' associations and professional societies (radiologic technologists, CRNAs, claims adjusters, AV teleoperators and safety drivers) as distribution partners. Members pay through a dues add-on, or employers buy it as a retention benefit.
problem: Regulations and enterprise policies demand 'meaningful human oversight', which in practice makes the human the liability sponge, the 'moral crumple zone'. Uber's Tempe safety driver was criminally charged, and nurse RaDonda Vaught was convicted after overriding an automated dispensing cabinet. Employer indemnities and malpractice policies rarely cover AI-specific disputes, licensing-board action, or retaliation for raising concerns.
solution: (1) A prepaid legal defense retainer covering civil, licensing-board and criminal matters, with panel counsel experienced in tech-mediated harm. (2) 'Override receipts': a light app or extension where the member logs each override, disagreement or safety concern, with hashed timestamps in a member-owned escrow. (3) Plain-English 'working with this AI tool' duty briefings per workplace system. (4) Aggregated, anonymised incident data that gives unions leverage in bargaining over staffing and AI use.
why_now: AI decision support is now standard in hospitals (sepsis alerts, ambient scribes) and in robotaxi remote operations. Human-oversight duties are being written into the EU AI Act and state laws. Insurers' AI exclusions signal to employers that AI losses may be uninsured, so risk will be pushed down to individual workers. Unions are actively bargaining over AI in 2025-26.
revenue_model: $9-19 per member per month through associations, with margin after panel counsel and a reinsurer or legal-plan administrator. Employer-paid group plans and individual upsells.
non_obvious_insight: The person who actually absorbs AI risk is neither the deployer nor the vendor but the individual signer, and no product exists for them. Unions already have distribution and every reason to buy. The override-receipt record may be worth more than the defense cover, because it is the human-oversight evidence courts will look for, and it hands the union data on unsafe deployments.
first_30_days: Pick one narrow group, such as AV teleoperators and safety drivers or nurses in one state. Get an MOU with one union local or association. Retain a defense-firm panel at group rates. Ship the override log as a Chrome extension or SMS bot. Pre-sell 300 members at $12 per month, and check state prepaid-legal-plan rules first.

title: NOI Haircut Reports for Multifamily Underwriting
one_liner: A 24-hour diligence report that restates a multifamily property's NOI for real concessions, renewal cliffs and banned fee income, sold to the lenders and buyers who will feel it first.
customer: Debt funds, CRE CLO managers, agency-lender underwriting teams and mid-market syndicators buying 100-1,000 unit properties in concession-heavy or fee-regulated markets.
problem: Headline NOI rests on face rents and other income. Concessions run 15.8% of stabilized units and 1.2M units are still in lease-up, and leases signed with free months renew at face rent a year later, inviting churn. Fee income (admin, pet, package, parking) is being banned: Seattle from July 2027 with treble damages, and the NAA tracked 140 fee bills in 2025. Sellers' T-12s show neither risk.
solution: Upload rent roll, T-12 and fee schedule and receive net-effective rent by lease cohort, concession burn-off and renewal-cliff dates, fee income at risk by jurisdiction and effective date, and a stressed NOI and DSCR. A monitoring API flags changes across a loan book as laws pass.
why_now: Concessions are now the pricing lever because rent cuts hurt valuations and algorithmic pricing is legally constrained. Dated fee bans give lenders a hard clock, and the rental supply wave has crested, so underwriting errors will show up in 2027 renewals.
revenue_model: $750-2,500 per report; $2-5K per monitored loan per year; enterprise API licenses to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: NOI has become a policy variable, but underwriting models still treat it as a market variable. The party whose model breaks first is the lender, not the operator, and lenders have diligence budgets.
first_30_days: Build a law and effective-date database for the 10 states and cities with fee rules. Publish three public teardown case studies on listed properties. Sell $500 pilot reports to 10 syndicators via LinkedIn and BiggerPockets, then pitch two debt funds on a diligence add-on.

title: AI-Aware E&O Cover for Solo Consultants
one_liner: A specialty insurance agency for laid-off professionals turned solo consultants whose errors-and-omissions cover may quietly exclude AI-assisted work, with premiums discounted for logged verification workflows.
customer: Solo and 2-10-person consultancies (fractional CFOs, marketing and analytics freelancers, dev contractors, HR and ops consultants) pay $400-1,500 a year in premium. The agency earns roughly 15-20% commission.
problem: Large carriers have reportedly sought AI-liability exclusions, so a freelancer who used AI on a deliverable can find a claim denied. Client contracts increasingly demand E&O plus AI-use reps. Newly independent laid-off professionals never read the policy language.
solution: A retail agency that places policies with carriers offering affirmative AI coverage (an MGA program later). A lightweight verification log (source checks, review sign-off) yields an underwriting-friendly attestation that lowers price. A contract clause checker flags indemnities, plus a template AI-use disclosure for clients.
why_now: Carrier AI-exclusion filings surfaced in late 2025, layoffs are creating a wave of new independents, and enterprise procurement now asks vendors for AI-use attestations. AI-liability startups target enterprises, not solos.
revenue_model: Commissions of 15-20%, MGA fees later, and a $10-a-month verification-log tool.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is one of underwriting information: how AI-assisted work is actually verified versus what the policy assumes. A logged verification workflow is data an insurer will pay for with lower prices. Premiums are too small for big brokers to chase, so a new insured class goes unserved.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed E&O producer (or get licensed). Read the AI language of 10 carriers and publish a 'Does your E&O cover AI?' checker and newsletter for laid-off and freelancer communities. Bind the first 20 policies.

title: Grant Recovery Desk for Small Cities
one_liner: A contingency-fee grant compliance and reimbursement service for small cities receiving FEMA, DOJ and counter-drone money with no staff to document it.
customer: Towns and counties with populations of 5-100K, especially those receiving disaster reimbursements and new safety grants (for example the $500M FEMA counter-UAS program).
problem: Small governments lose federal reimbursements to incomplete documentation, procurement missteps and audit findings. With federal agencies shrinking and reorganizations stalled in court, help is thinner. Dallas County is cutting IT staff, and local budgets are tight.
solution: A software-plus-service program that structures the grant lifecycle: eligibility check, procurement compliance, receipt capture, quarterly reporting and closeout audit packages. It uses AI to read award terms and flag non-compliant purchases before they happen. Paid from recovered funds.
why_now: New grant streams (counter-drone, cyber, disaster) are landing at localities while federal grant-management staff are being cut. Regulators enforce documentation harder as budgets tighten.
revenue_model: Contingency of 4-8% of recovered or protected award dollars, with a minimum retainer. A city with $2M in awards yields about $80-160K.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer pays nothing up front, and the alternative is losing money already awarded. Contingency pricing turns a dreaded compliance cost into free money for a small clerk's office.
first_30_days: Offer free award-file reviews to 10 small cities identified from public award lists. Build a compliance checklist per program. Sign 2 contingency deals.

title: Placement Exchange for Clients PE Firms Shed
one_liner: A compliant offboarding and warm-handoff service that places small clients dropped by PE-backed accounting firms with vetted independent bookkeepers.
customer: PE-backed and roll-up accounting platforms that raise fee minimums and prune small clients, and independent bookkeepers, enrolled agents and CPAs who want more clients.
problem: PE roll-ups push firms toward larger clients (prior knowledge, not re-verified), so thousands of micro-clients get a 30-day termination letter with scattered records. The exiting firm has E&O and reputation exposure, and the clients don't know where to go. Independent shops want clients but cannot find or vet them. CPA supply is flat at about 678,000.
solution: An offboarding workflow for the shedding firm: client consent, export of prior-year returns and workpapers, engagement-letter templates, and a warm handoff to independents matched on industry, software, language and location. Receiving firms are vetted and rated, and there is a service-level guarantee if the client is unhappy.
why_now: Multi-year PE consolidation of accounting firms continues, AI reduces cost-to-serve for large clients faster than small ones, and the CPA pipeline is flat while demand is projected to rise.
revenue_model: $150-400 per placed client from the receiving firm, $50-100 per client offboarding fee from the shedding firm, and later 8-10% of first-year fees as a recurring referral.
non_obvious_insight: For the roll-up, shedding small clients is an unpriced cost center with legal exposure, so it will pay for graceful exits. The demand side is a waiting list of independents.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 independent bookkeepers and EAs as the buyer panel. Approach operations leaders at five regional roll-ups and offer a free pilot for 50 pruned clients. Build the export checklist and record acceptance and satisfaction rates.

title: Lake Ice Posts for Ice-Fishing Resorts
one_liner: Cheap solar LoRa thermistor-chain posts frozen into lake ice along access routes, giving resort operators and snowmobile clubs a live thickness trend and rate-of-change alerts on a seasonal subscription.
customer: Ice-fishing resorts and outfitters that rent ice houses and plow ice roads (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, Maine, Ontario), snowmobile clubs that groom lake trails, ice-derby and tournament organizers, lake associations and rescue units.
problem: Ice thickness varies across a lake and changes fast with warm rain, currents and springs. Resorts rely on daily manual auger checks at a few points. Vehicle and ice-house losses, and deaths, happen. Recent low-ice winters make timing harder. Research-grade buoys exist but cost far too much for a resort, and crowdsourced apps can't watch one specific corridor.
solution: A roughly USD 150 solar post with a thermistor chain spanning air, ice and water, plus a tilt sensor. It infers ice thickness from the 0 degree C interface and gradient, calibrated against the operator's own auger readings. Deploy 3-6 posts along the access road and ice-house village. The dashboard uses plain thresholds by vehicle class, texts an alert on rapid thinning, and offers an embeddable public 'ice conditions' widget for the resort's website.
why_now: It is late September, so units built now can be frozen in for this winter's first ice. LoRa, solar and thermistor chains are commodity. Ice-data apps (satellite radar, crowd reports) prove operators will pay for information, and research-grade buoys have validated the concept, leaving a low-cost tier open.
revenue_model: USD 199 hardware, plus USD 99-249 per post per season. Resort bundle of USD 1,500-4,000 per season. Sponsorship of the public widget by bait shops and outdoor brands. Contract work for counties and rescue units.
non_obvious_insight: Don't sell 'is the ice safe,' which is uncertifiable and a liability trap. Sell operational due diligence and a rate-of-change early warning: ice fails by trend (thermal decay, current), and a fixed post sees the trend before a weekly auger check does. Resorts lose money and reputation when they close roads early or lose a vehicle, so revenue protection is the wedge.
first_30_days: Build 25 posts before first freeze from off-the-shelf thermistor strings, LoRa boards and small solar panels. Sign 4-5 resorts to shoulder-season pilots at cost. Use their daily auger logs as ground truth. Launch a free public ice map to collect crowd calibration points and sponsors. Convert to season subscriptions and use winter data for next year's preorder round.

title: Public-Access TV Stations Become Media Notaries
angle: Pairing 2: Creator economy & media provenance x Government/public sector/defense/municipal services (human-made proof x municipal media infrastructure)
one_liner: Convert struggling PEG community-media centers into witnessed-recording and signing hubs that cities pay to certify official meeting video and creators pay to prove a recording was performed live by a human in a real room.
customer: City and county clerks ($300-600/month for signed, canonical video of meetings, hearings and emergency briefings), PEG access centers (keep about 60% as delivery partners), and local musicians, podcasters and hyperlocal news creators ($45 per witnessed session or $15/month for verified-clip embeds). Later buyers are sync buyers and ad agencies.
problem: PEG centers (public, educational and government access TV) are funded by cable franchise fees that erode as cable subscriptions fall (prior knowledge), yet they own studios, gear, staff and a role recording local government. Meanwhile fully AI tracks passed 50% of Deezer uploads (July 2026), AI-cloned officials' clips circulate, platform human badges are free and per-artist (Spotify) or absent (YouTube will not demote labeled AI), and detectors are only probabilistic. Nobody sells 'this was made live, in this room, on this date, witnessed by a public institution'.
solution: A roughly $600 witness kit plus software: hardware-signed capture into C2PA manifests, staff-attested session logs with an ID check of performers, and raw timestamped multitrack takes. Cities get a canonical signed meeting archive and a public 'verify this clip' page. Local news creators embed verified clips, and artists attach a 'Recorded live at [Center], [date]' credential to releases and distributor metadata.
why_now: EU AI Act Article 50 marking and disclosure duties started applying 2026-08-02. C2PA 2.3 and TikTok's July 2026 steering-committee entry mean signed media can now travel across platforms. Platforms went from tolerating to policing AI in months (Bandcamp ban, Spotify AI Persona labels, TIDAL demonetization), and PEG funding pressure means centers need new revenue lines.
revenue_model: City subscriptions, per-session fees split with PEG centers, an annual software license to centers, and later per-clip verification fees from sync buyers.
non_obvious_insight: A credential is only as trustworthy as the institution behind it. Platforms cannot referee because they sell AI tools, and detectors give probabilities while a witness gives testimony. PEG centers are the only neutral, government-adjacent, physically distributed and already-recording institutions in most towns, and their core asset is exactly what provenance lacks: a place and a person willing to attest.
first_30_days: Contact the Alliance for Community Media state chapters and equip 3 PEG stations in one state. Sign one month of council meetings free, then demo a deepfaked council clip against the signed original to sell a $300/month city plan. Open 'Witnessed Live' studio hours to 20 local artists at $45.

title: Post-Montgomery Walk-Around Audits for Freight Brokers
one_liner: A gig network of working and retired truckers who physically inspect the carriers a broker hires and hand back a lawyer-ready diligence file.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers and 3PLs ($50M to $1B gross bookings, 10 to 200 staff). The budget owner is the VP of compliance/risk or general counsel. Secondary buyers are contingent-auto and broker E&O underwriters, and shippers that run in-house brokerage.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-selection suits against brokers are not preempted by federal law. Brokers now have to prove they exercised reasonable care picking a carrier. Their vetting is entirely digital: SAFER lookups, insurance certificates, ID checks. Nobody has ever looked at the yard. Chameleon carriers with clean paperwork, fake addresses and fictitious pickups sail through, and so do genuinely dangerous small fleets. Verisk CargoNet put Q2 2026 theft losses at $304.6M, more than double Q2 2025, even though incident counts fell.
solution: Book a 45-minute physical walk-around of a carrier's listed terminal, yard or the driver's truck for $175 to $350. The trucker follows a 40-point protocol and shoots geo-stamped photo and video: steer tire tread and sidewall damage, brake chamber stroke, lights, ELD present and working, trailer age and VIN against registration, whether the address has a shop, lot and signage, and a two-minute driver interview. The broker gets a scored, reproducible report filed against the carrier ID. Upsells are a quarterly re-walk for top-tier carriers on high-risk lanes, and 'eyes on pickup', where a local trucker sits at the shipper's dock and confirms the right driver and truck load the freight (aimed at high-value copper, electronics and pharma loads). Build the checklist with a trucking-defense attorney so it holds up as evidence.
why_now: The May 2026 Montgomery ruling created a brand-new legal duty and every broker general counsel is scrambling. Insurers are repricing broker liability. Fictitious-pickup and impersonation theft keeps growing (Verisk CargoNet counted 158 fictitious pickups in Q2 2026). Meanwhile English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement and the February 2026 non-domiciled CDL rule are churning the small-carrier population, so more unknown carriers are entering the market.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees of $175 to $350, with the trucker keeping about 45 to 55%. Annual diligence-program retainers of $25k to $100k for brokers that want a defined audit cadence. Insurer premium-credit revenue share. A recurring data subscription selling carrier physical-condition scores back to the wider broker market.
non_obvious_insight: Any 20-year driver can size up a carrier's yard in 90 seconds. Chameleon outfits have one shiny truck, no shop, mismatched trailers, cords showing on the steer tires, and drivers who can't name their dispatcher. Digital vetting checks paperwork; a jury after Montgomery will ask 'did anyone actually look?' The product isn't a tool, it's discoverable proof of reasonable care. Drivers are already within 30 miles of nearly any carrier and sit idle on 34-hour restarts and at detention, so the inspector supply is cheaper and more credible than any consultancy's.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 vetted current and retired drivers from CDL forums and trucker Facebook groups and pay them per audit. Pay a trucking-defense attorney $2k to $3k to co-design the checklist and co-brand a 'Montgomery diligence protocol'. Build the capture app as a PWA with forms, geotagged photos and an auto-generated PDF. Cold-email 40 mid-size broker GCs and compliance heads, offering 5 pilot audits at $99 on their riskiest tier-3 carriers. Target 3 paying brokers by day 30 and 100 audits by month 3.

title: Night-Shift Bench Techs for Time-Critical Experiments
one_liner: An agency of vetted, laid-off bench technicians who show up at 2 a.m. or on Christmas morning to harvest time points, feed cells and load overnight runs from the lab's own protocol cards, with photo proof and a break-glass line to the postdoc.
customer: Small private biotechs and startups in shared lab space (LabCentral-type incubators and coworking labs), plus soft-money academic labs with reagent or staffing budgets and industry-funded academic labs. Billed at $85-120/hour with a 2-hour minimum. The incubator or landlord earns a referral fee.
problem: Biology runs on its own clock. 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. time-course harvests, weekend and holiday cell feeding, 48-hour induction windows and overnight instrument runs are the hidden cost of every wet-lab career. Postdocs cover them with sleep debt, guilt-based favors from grad students, or driving in on Christmas. The person who could do it is often laid off, but a lab will not hand $40k of iPSC-derived cells to a stranger, and access badges and insurance make casual help impossible.
solution: A W-2 (employer-of-record) pool of experienced techs, aseptic-technique certified and proven on a practice run, working from the customer's 'protocol cards'. Each shift is a fixed product: Time-Point Harvest, Weekend Split and Feed, Holiday Cover, Overnight Run Loader. Each has a checklist, timestamped photos at every step, a pre-shift 30-minute video walkthrough, and a break-glass contact. Sitters first do a 'dry run' on the customer's cheap spare line. Incubator and coworking-lab operators put the agency on an approved-vendor list, which solves badge and insurance access once for hundreds of labs.
why_now: A large pool of experienced bench techs and postdocs has been released by biotech layoffs since 2023 and funding disruption in 2025-26. Lean startups have fewer people per experiment, so time-critical work lands on founders. Bigger time-course, organoid and perturbation experiments driven by AI-bio data demand make odd-hour work more frequent. Shared-lab operators want more amenities to fill vacant benches.
revenue_model: A markup on billed hours (techs are paid about $40-55/hour, the agency bills $85-120). Monthly retainer for guaranteed availability (for example 'holiday cover pass'). Referral revenue share from shared-lab operators.
non_obvious_insight: The hard constraint is trust, not skill. Nobody outsources their cells because failure is invisible until weeks later. So the product is really an evidence-and-liability wrapper: photo proof, protocol cards, dry runs, and operator pre-approval. Also, the early customers are not academia (IACUC, badges and university procurement kill it) but private benches in rented lab space, where one operator agreement unlocks dozens of labs.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 recently laid-off techs through personal networks and biotech alumni groups. Get a business license, a staffing or PEO partner for payroll, and general liability insurance. Call the community managers at 2-3 shared-lab spaces in one city and offer the first holiday-cover week free. Sell the first paid 3 a.m. harvest to a founder who is already doing it themselves. Turn every job into a reusable protocol card. Aim for about 10 recurring customers by month 6.

title: Pre-Registered Neighbor Impact Studies for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral 'testing lab' for whether a data center, battery plant or transmission line lowers nearby home values, with the method locked and published before anyone sees the results.
customer: Four payers. (1) Data center, BESS, solar and transmission developers facing moratoria or rezoning hearings pay $15-60k per study. (2) County and city planning departments and utility commissions pay $10-40k for a neutral study. (3) Resident coalitions and HOAs pay $3-8k for a 'lite' study, usually crowdfunded. (4) Landowner condemnation and easement attorneys.
problem: Every land-use fight ends in dueling consultant reports. Developer studies use hand-picked matched pairs that always show 'no impact'. Residents bring anecdotes. Planning staff can't judge either side, so boards vote on vibes and moratoria spread. Nobody trusts any report, so the reports are worthless.
solution: A repeatable, pre-registered protocol. Step 1: publish (timestamped and hashed) the analysis plan, including radius bands, event dates and exclusion rules. Step 2: pull every arm's-length sale within 0.25 to 2 miles, before and after the announcement date and the operation date. Step 3: run a repeat-sales difference-in-differences or synthetic-control analysis against similar areas that had no project. Step 4: have a licensed appraiser review every sale for arm's-length status, condition and segment (estates, REO and investor flips get pulled), and do a ground visit for what is actually audible and visible from the homes. Step 5: deliver a USPAP-compliant consulting report plus an interactive map. Results are published whichever way they come out. Add a 5-year 'impact monitor' subscription for counties and developers that tracks post-operation sales.
why_now: AI-driven data center siting in 2025-26 has produced local moratoria, rezoning denials and noise complaints in many states (VA, GA, TX, AZ, IN, OH). Property values are one of the top arguments alongside power and water. Federal and state pushes to speed up transmission and energy siting mean more condemnation and easement fights. Public sales data plus cheap compute make a rigorous study a $10k job instead of a $100k one.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee studies, paid upfront into escrow so the client cannot steer the result. Annual retainers for repeat developers (for example 8-10 sites a year). $10-15k/yr monitoring subscriptions for counties. Later, an 'Impact Study Standard' certification that planning codes can reference.
non_obvious_insight: Appraisers know matched-pair studies are the hired gun's favorite toy: pick 6 pairs that support the client and you're done, and both sides know it. Credibility is the scarce input, not analysis. Pre-registration is standard in clinical trials and unheard of in appraisal. Developers will pay for a study that might go against them, because a study nobody believes is worth nothing at a hearing. The other secret is timing. Buyer perception moves at announcement, before the first shovel, so studies run only on 'after operation' miss the effect. A difference-in-differences on the announcement date catches it.
first_30_days: Pick one hot metro (for example Northern Virginia or metro Atlanta). Run a free 'shadow study' on existing data centers there using public sales records, with the method pre-registered on a public page. Email planning directors, 10 resident groups and 5 developer permitting leads. Recruit two appraisers as signing reviewers. Aim to sign one $12-20k study, or a county pilot, by day 30-45.
